clinicalPearls: A photosensitive, non-scarring cutaneous lupus subtype presenting in two morphologies: annular polycyclic lesions and papulosquamous (psoriasiform) plaques, favouring the upper back, shoulders, extensor arms and V of the neck while sparing the mid-face and knuckles.
Strongly associated with anti-Ro/SSA (and often anti-La/SSB) antibodies; most patients are anti-Ro positive.
Lesions characteristically heal without scarring but often leave persistent dyspigmentation and telangiectasia; central clearing gives annular lesions a distinctive rim.
A large proportion of cases are drug-induced, classically by thiazides, terbinafine, calcium-channel blockers, proton-pump inhibitors, antifungals, TNF inhibitors and chemotherapy agents.
Only a minority meet full criteria for systemic lupus erythematosus, and systemic involvement, when present, tends to be mild; nonetheless screening for systemic disease is essential.
Anti-Ro positivity carries a risk of neonatal lupus and congenital heart block in offspring, so pregnancy planning and fetal monitoring are important.
Photoprotection and photosensitivity counselling are cornerstones, since ultraviolet light reliably provokes and worsens lesions.
Antimalarials such as hydroxychloroquine are first-line systemic therapy, alongside topical corticosteroids and calcineurin inhibitors; smoking reduces antimalarial efficacy.
reference.pathophysiology: Subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus is an autoimmune interface dermatitis in which ultraviolet radiation, particularly UVB, drives keratinocyte apoptosis and translocation of intracellular Ro/SSA antigen to the cell surface. Anti-Ro/SSA autoantibodies then bind these exposed antigens, promoting antibody-dependent and cytotoxic T-cell-mediated destruction of basal keratinocytes at the dermo-epidermal junction. A type I interferon-rich milieu amplifies the response, and genetic predisposition (including HLA associations and complement deficiencies) increases susceptibility. Photosensitivity is therefore intrinsic to the disease mechanism. Numerous systemic drugs can trigger or unmask SCLE, presumably by enhancing photosensitivity or altering keratinocyte antigen expression, producing lesions clinically and serologically indistinguishable from idiopathic disease that typically remit after the culprit drug is withdrawn. Because the inflammatory attack is centred on the basal layer rather than the deeper appendages, lesions resolve without the dermal scarring and follicular destruction that characterise discoid lupus, though pigmentary change frequently persists.
additionalDifferentials: Discoid lupus erythematosus and other chronic cutaneous lupus variants
Tinea corporis and other annular dermatoses (granuloma annulare, erythema annulare centrifugum)
Polymorphic light eruption and other photodermatoses
additionalInvestigations: Anti-Ro/SSA and anti-La/SSB antibodies with a full antinuclear antibody panel
Skin biopsy with histology showing interface dermatitis and direct immunofluorescence
Complement levels, full blood count, renal function and urinalysis to screen for systemic lupus
Detailed drug history and medication review for photosensitising culprit agents
Antiphospholipid antibody testing where thrombotic or obstetric risk is a concern
Assessment for neonatal lupus risk and fetal cardiac monitoring in anti-Ro-positive pregnancy
redFlags: Features suggesting systemic lupus such as nephritis, cytopenias, serositis or neuropsychiatric symptoms
New or worsening eruption temporally linked to a recently started photosensitising drug
Anti-Ro positivity in pregnancy given the risk of congenital heart block
Extensive or rapidly progressive disease unresponsive to first-line therapy
reference.prognosis: The cutaneous prognosis is generally favourable, with non-scarring lesions that respond to photoprotection and antimalarials and, in drug-induced cases, remit after withdrawal of the culprit. A minority progress to or coexist with systemic lupus, so ongoing surveillance is warranted.
pitfalls: Overlooking a drug trigger and continuing the offending photosensitising medication
Assuming all cutaneous lupus is systemic, or conversely failing to screen for systemic involvement
Missing anti-Ro-related neonatal lupus and heart-block risk in women of childbearing age
Confusing papulosquamous SCLE with psoriasis and treating with agents that may aggravate lupus
Neglecting rigorous photoprotection and smoking cessation, which undermines antimalarial response
